title: Test statistics and their null distribution
keyIdea: A test statistic is a quantity calculated from the sample that is used to test H₀. In a binomial test it is X, the number of successes in n trials, not the parameter p. Its null distribution is the distribution X would have if H₀ were true: X ~ B(n, p₀), where n is the number of trials and p₀ is the value stated in H₀, never the sample proportion. The binomial model needs a fixed n, two outcomes, independent trials and a constant p. The null distribution depends only on H₀ and n, so it tells you which results are ordinary and which would be rare if H₀ were true.
familyTip: Ask your teenager how they would test whether a dice rolls too many sixes. What would they count? What distribution would that count have if the dice were fair? Then ask why the distribution uses 1/6 and not the proportion of sixes they actually rolled.

visual.caption: Which numbers go into the null distribution X ~ B(n, p₀)? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pick the test statistic, build X ~ B(n, p₀), simulate H₀, check binomial conditions, move H₀ under fixed data, and read tails.

kid: A hypothesis test needs one number from the sample to judge the claim. That number is the test statistic. In a binomial test it is X, the count of successes: the sixes in 60 rolls, or the faulty bolts in 50. The parameter p is not the statistic. It belongs to the whole population, and H₀ makes a claim about it.

Next, write down how X would behave if H₀ were true. This is the null distribution. For 60 rolls of a dice with H₀: p = 1/6, it is X ~ B(60, 1/6). The n is the number of trials. The p is the value in H₀, not the share you saw. If you rolled 15 sixes, 15/60 is your evidence, so it cannot also be the model you test it against.

Why assume H₀? Because we need a fixed model to measure surprise. If you simulate a fair coin tossed 20 times, again and again, most head counts land near np = 10. A count of 17 hardly ever happens, so seeing 17 would be strong evidence against a fair coin.

Check that a binomial model fits: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, independent trials and the same p every time. Counting rolls until the first six fails, because n is not fixed. Changing H₀ moves the null distribution, but your data stay exactly where they were.
adult: Ages 16 to 18. This is A level Mathematics statistics: students state the test statistic and its distribution under H₀ for a binomial test, for example X ~ B(20, 0.5). It follows from writing H₀ and H₁, and leads on to p-values and critical regions, which are both tail probabilities of this distribution.

The terms. A test statistic is calculated from sample data. The null distribution is its sampling distribution when H₀ is true. For a binomial test, X ~ B(n, p₀) with mean np₀ and variance np₀(1 − p₀). It needs fixed n, two outcomes, independence and constant p. Sampling without replacement from a small population breaks independence.

Common mistakes. Students give the parameter p, or the number of trials, as the test statistic. They put the sample proportion into B(n, p) instead of p₀, or swap the observed count and n (B(15, 1/6)). Some think H₀ is assumed because it is true. Others forget to define X in context, which mark schemes require.

In the lab students choose the test statistic for four contexts and build the null distribution for three by tapping n and p. They run 300 simulations of a fair coin and watch them match B(20, 0.5). They sort six situations by whether a binomial model fits. Then they drag H₀'s p while the observed 14 stays put, and read P(X ≥ x) for 13, 15 and 17 heads.

practice.prompt: A dice is rolled 60 times to test whether it shows six too often. What is the test statistic?
choices: X, the number of sixes in the 60 rolls
p, the probability of a six
60, the number of rolls
practice.hint: The statistic is calculated from the sample. Which of these is counted?
practice.explain: X counts sixes in the sample. p is the parameter H₀ makes a claim about, and 60 is the fixed number of trials.

practice.prompt: Under H₀, X ~ B({=2*m}, 0.5). What is the mean of the null distribution?
practice.hint: The mean of B(n, p) is np.
practice.explain: np = {=2*m} × 0.5 = {m}. If H₀ is true, counts near {m} are ordinary.

practice.prompt: 60 rolls give 15 sixes. H₀: p = 1/6. What is the distribution of X under H₀?
practice.hint: n is the number of trials; p comes from H₀.
practice.explain: There are 60 trials and H₀ says p = 1/6, so X ~ B(60, 1/6). 1/4 is the sample proportion 15/60, and 15 is the observed count.

practice.prompt: Under H₀, X ~ B({=4*m}, 0.5). What is the variance of X?
practice.hint: The variance of B(n, p) is np(1 − p).

practice.prompt: Which count cannot be modelled by a binomial distribution?
choices: The number of rolls needed to get the first six
The number of heads in 50 coin tosses
The number of 40 patients who recover, each independently with chance 0.7
practice.hint: Check each condition: fixed n, two outcomes, independence, constant p.
practice.explain: Rolling until the first six has no fixed number of trials, so it is not binomial. The other two meet every condition.

pool.prompt: Red comes up 9 times in 40 spins. H₀: p = 0.3. What is the null distribution?
pool.hint: Use the number of spins and the p in H₀.
pool.explain: n = 40 spins and p₀ = 0.3 from H₀. 0.225 = 9/40 is the sample proportion, which is the evidence, not the model.

pool.prompt: Why is the null distribution worked out assuming H₀ is true?
choices: To see how likely the observed result would be if H₀ held
Because H₀ has been proved true
Because the data always agree with H₀
pool.hint: What does the test need a fixed model for?
pool.explain: H₀ is assumed, not known. The model shows which results would be ordinary or rare if H₀ held, so the data can be judged against it.

pool.prompt: In a test of whether over 2% of bolts are faulty, 50 bolts are checked. What is the test statistic?
choices: X, the number of faulty bolts in the 50
The time until the first faulty bolt
pool.hint: A binomial test counts successes in a fixed number of trials.
pool.explain: X counts faulty bolts in the sample of 50. 0.02 is the H₀ value of the parameter, and a waiting time is not a binomial count.

pool.prompt: The same data are tested against H₀: p = 0.3 instead of H₀: p = 0.5. What changes?
choices: The null distribution
The observed value of X
The number of trials
pool.hint: Which of these depends on H₀?
pool.explain: The null distribution is B(n, p₀), so a new p₀ moves it. The data and n were fixed by the experiment.

pool.prompt: Under H₀, X ~ B({=10*m}, 0.1). What is the expected value of X?
pool.hint: For X ~ B(n, p), the expected value is E(X) = np.

pool.prompt: A spinner should land on blue with probability 0.25. It is spun {=4*m} times to test this. What is the mean of X under H₀?
pool.hint: Write X ~ B(n, 0.25), then use np.

pool.prompt: Under H₀: p = 0.5, X ~ B(20, 0.5) and P(X ≥ 15) ≈ 0.021. What does this mean?
choices: 15 or more heads would be rare if the coin were fair
The coin has a 2.1% chance of being fair
H₀ is true 97.9% of the time
pool.hint: The probability is worked out assuming H₀.
pool.explain: It is the chance of 15 or more heads if H₀ is true. It is not the probability that H₀ is true.

pool.prompt: 5 cards are dealt from one pack without replacement and the hearts counted. Why is B(5, 1/4) not exact?
choices: The chance of a heart changes after each card, so trials are not independent
There are more than two suits
5 is too few trials for any binomial
pool.hint: Does each card have the same chance of being a heart?
pool.explain: Without replacement the chance of a heart changes as cards are dealt, so the trials are not independent with constant p.

pool.prompt: Which is the best definition of the null distribution?
choices: The distribution of the test statistic if H₀ is true
The distribution of the sample data you collected
The distribution of p after the test
pool.hint: Null refers to H₀. Which option describes the statistic under H₀?
pool.explain: It is how the test statistic would vary from sample to sample if H₀ were true, such as X ~ B(20, 0.5).
